q: When gathering a behavioural history at intake, which pair of communication skills reduces social desirability bias?
o: Direct interrogation and closed-ended metrics
Active listening and the use of objective language
Subjective interpretation and passive recording
Validated trait rating and ad-libitum notation
e: Intake staff should ask open-ended questions, use objective language, and apply active listening to get accurate disclosures.

q: Which is named as a primary source of environmental unpredictability that drives chronic fear and anxiety?
o: Using a population manager to lead daily rounds
Irregular patterns of continuous light or darkness
Providing a choice of resources in group housing
Giving fast-acting psychopharmacology before intake
e: The three drivers are lack of routine, frequent disruption of enclosure set-up, and irregular patterns of continuous light or darkness.

q: On the 103-item C-BARQ, assuring owners of confidentiality made them more likely to disclose which behaviours?
o: Separation-related and attachment-seeking behaviours
Aggression toward family members or fear of strangers
Stranger-directed aggression and non-social fear
Dog-directed aggression and resource guarding
e: Confidentiality increased disclosure of family-directed aggression and fear of strangers; other categories showed no difference.

q: Using the shorter 42-item C-BARQ, what was the effect of confidentiality assurances on disclosure?
o: It doubled disclosure of human-directed bites
It eliminated social desirability bias entirely
There was no difference between the confidential and non-confidential groups
Owners became far less forthcoming for fear of euthanasia
e: The 42-item version showed no difference, unlike the 103-item version. Self-administered tools may still reduce bias, but evidence is incomplete.

q: At two weeks post-adoption, which behaviours correlate with surrender reports?
o: Barking, house soiling, and predatory drive
Fear, anxiety, or aggression toward vets, and aggression toward unfamiliar people
Kennel spinning and stereotypic pacing
Tail tucked and food-bowl freezing
e: At 2 weeks, aggression toward unfamiliar people, urination when alone, and destructive chewing correlate with surrender reports.

q: How do post-adoption correlations change from the 2-week to the 6-week follow-up?
o: They increase sharply due to trigger stacking
There are fewer correlations, limited mainly to aggression toward unfamiliar people, urination when alone, and destructive chewing
Resource guarding becomes the single predictor of return
Adopter reports lose all alignment with shelter observations
e: By 6 weeks there are fewer correlations overall, with only a few behaviours still matching surrender reports.

q: Close to 80% of dogs are fearful at the vet. For a dog reported fearful at a vet exam, what is the correlated chance of fear in new situations?
e: Dogs fearful at the vet (about 55% by owner report) show fear in new situations about 68% of the time.

q: A dog fearful at the veterinarian is statistically prone to which secondary presentations?
o: 35% pain or touch sensitivity and 37% non-social fear
75% human-directed biting and 20% kennel guarding
16% true aggression and 48% separation anxiety
60% food guarding and 50% conspecific reactivity
e: Vet-fearful dogs show pain or touch sensitivity about 35% of the time and non-social fear about 37%.

q: Why are untrained daily-care staff observations of behaviour often inaccurate?
o: They are trained only to monitor BCS and gait
People may be reluctant to disclose negative information that could hurt the dog's adoption chances
The observer effect eliminates their ability to see pacing
They use input-based rather than animal-based measures
e: A key reason is reluctance to report negatives that might jeopardise adoption. Staff predicted only about a third of later-reported problems.

q: Close to half of the shelter staff studied made which observational error?
o: Mistook fearful tracking for a stable trait
Mistook aggressive behaviour for excitement and frustration
Mistook play for chew-bone guarding
Classified non-aggressive behaviour as severe attacks
e: About half mistook aggression for excitement or frustration, but rarely the reverse, so people tend to judge dogs positively.

q: What physical focus differentiates trainers from non-experts when reading canine behaviour?
o: Non-experts watch the tail; trainers time vocalisations
Non-experts focus on the head; trainers attend to the body
Trainers track only HPA-axis parameters
Trainers watch the kennel front; non-experts watch hiding
e: Non-experts focus on the head, while trainers attend to the body and read motivation and emotion better. Training improves non-experts.

q: In which situation is a dog's probability of aggression toward people highest?
o: During offsite walks or field trips
With a moderately social stimulus dog
When confined to a kennel
During a standardised medical intake exam
e: Aggression toward people is highest in the kennel; aggression toward other dogs tends to be lowest there.

q: What are the cortisol peak timelines reported in shelter dogs?
o: Plasma peaks day 17; urine peaks days 1 to 3
Plasma is highest in the first 3 days; urinary peaks at 17 days
Both peak at exactly 5 days
Cortisol does not fluctuate with time
e: Plasma cortisol peaks in the first 3 days then declines; urinary cortisol peaks around day 17.

q: How does prior kenneling experience affect urinary cortisol?
o: It up-regulates the HPA axis and doubles cortisol
Dogs with prior kenneling experience have lower urine cortisol than naive dogs
It linearizes plasma cortisol
There is no correlation
e: Previously kenneled dogs show lower urinary cortisol than dogs with no such experience.

q: Why caution against using a dog's movement or body position as the sole marker of welfare?
o: Movement can only be measured by scan sampling
Behavioural stress is expressed in many ways and correlates poorly with plasma cortisol
Enclosure standards require a static posture
Posture is dictated only by nutrition and BCS
e: Behaviour is a weak sole stress marker because it varies widely and correlates poorly with plasma cortisol.

q: What is the primary diagnostic limitation of the ASPCA SAFER assessment?
o: A 100% false positive rate
It differentiates none/mild from severe aggression but misses MODERATE aggression
It needs over 60 minutes and 4 handlers
It relies on a Likert scale with severe bias
e: SAFER (sensitivity 60%, specificity 50%) misses dogs with moderate aggression.

q: The mAAP test (sensitivity 73%, specificity 59%) showed strong utility for which outcome?
o: Predicting time spent resting in the bed
Correlating evaluation aggression with owner reports
Identifying chew-bone guarding from a doll
Differentiating spinning from anhedonia
e: The mAAP correlated behavioural-assessment aggression well with owner reports.

q: What is the verified predictive value of the assess-a-hand food-guarding test for home behaviour?
o: It accurately predicts presence of severe home guarding
High positive but 0% negative predictive value
It predicts ABSENCE better: 78% of non-guarders in the test also did not guard at home
It correlates perfectly with owner-directed bites at 6 weeks
e: The test identifies non-guarders better than guarders; 78% of test non-guarders also did not guard at home.

q: In Patronek and Bradley's simulations, why is the false-positive share still about 48% even at 85% sensitivity and 85% specificity?
o: 85% accuracy cannot calculate negative predictive value
Aggression toward people is low prevalence, present in no more than 16% of dogs
The observer effect inflates urinary cortisol
Handlers fail to use a male tester
e: Low prevalence (16%) means many positives are false; even at 85%/85% the false-positive share stays near half, hence no better than flipping a coin.

q: For the threatening stranger test, which variable is controlled to maximise informational output?
o: Test inside group housing during feeding
The tester should ideally be male, since dogs are more reactive to men
The handler must drop the leash completely
Repeat the subtest 5 times a week with no rest days
e: The test is sensitive to tester sex and is most informative with a male tester.

q: Using a model (fake) dog to assess conspecific reactivity, agreement is lowest for which category?
o: Friendliness
Fearfulness
Playfulness
Aggressiveness
e: Model dogs show good agreement for friendliness, moderate for fearfulness, and poor for aggressiveness.

q: What timing does the text recommend for assessing owner-relinquished versus stray dogs?
o: Both on day 17 to match the urinary cortisol peak
Owner-relinquished at intake; strays the day before the end of the hold (or after day 3 if the hold exceeds 5 days)
Strays within 48 hours before plasma cortisol declines
Never until 2 weeks in foster
e: Assess surrenders at intake (reduces LOS); assess strays the day before hold ends, or after day 3 for holds over 5 days.

q: A structured feline behavioural test yields which quantitative metrics?
o: Agreeableness, extraversion, neuroticism on a Likert matrix
Rating of severity (1 to 5), frequency, duration, proportion, and latency
Presence or absence of tracking across ad-libitum scans
Air quality, temperature, and enclosure size
e: Structured tests rate severity (1 to 5) plus frequency, duration, proportion, and latency of a behaviour.

q: What is the primary limitation of the Feline Temperament Profile (FTP)?
o: Scores change drastically after adoption
It cannot be completed within 30 minutes
It is not designed to identify a propensity for specific undesirable behaviours
It requires invasive plasma sampling
e: The FTP is valid and consistent but is not built to flag specific undesirable behaviours.

q: What critical caveat applies to the ASPCA Feline-ality assessment scales?
o: It increases LOS and raises euthanasia
It needs a behaviourist familiar with the cat
As of yet, no studies have evaluated the reliability or validity of these scales in shelters
It forces food-guarding triggers that cause trigger stacking
e: Despite operational benefits, the reliability and validity of the Feline-ality scales in shelters are not yet established.

q: Which framework organises care into Good feeding, Good housing, Good health, and Appropriate behaviour?
o: The Five Freedoms
The Welfare Quality 4 Principles
The Five Domains Model
The LIMA Humane Hierarchy
e: Those four are the Welfare Quality principles, distinct from the Five Freedoms and Five Domains.

q: What does Qualitative Behaviour Assessment (QBA) measure to gauge affective state?
o: Frequency of stereotypic spinning over 24 hours
The expressivity of the whole animal as it engages with its environment
The ratio of urinary to plasma cortisol
Distance maintained from a hiding box
e: QBA assesses whole-animal expressivity and shows high inter-rater agreement, capturing the affective state better than breaking behaviour into parts.

q: Why is a hiding box one of the most impactful modifications for newly admitted cats?
o: It lets staff do trait ratings without the observer effect
It removes the need for daily cleaning
It facilitates a quicker reduction in stress, so cats approach the cage front more and spend less time behind the litter box
It replaces psychopharmacology
e: Hiding boxes speed stress reduction; box cats approached the cage front more and hid behind the litter box less.

q: Who must be on the daily rounds team, and when should rounds ideally occur?
o: The surrendering owner and a legal consultant, after adoption hours
Representatives from operations, medical, and behaviour, conducted before cleaning and feeding
Certified trainers only, during 17-day cycles
Volunteers and fosterers, during offsite trips
e: Rounds include operations, medical, and behaviour perspectives and are done before cleaning and feeding to catch inappetent animals.

q: How should the team respond to stereotypic or repetitive behaviours in the population?
o: Immediately prescribe long-term medication to mask the signs
Address the fundamental causes by reducing stressors and changing the environment, rather than ad-hoc treatment of signs
Increase standardised testing to force an outcome
Restrict the animal's choice and control to prevent trigger stacking
e: Target the root causes (reduce stressors, change the environment); pharmacology should not replace environmental change.
